newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan seeks big Libyan debts.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan seeks big Libyan debts.

text.p: Islamist Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan on Wednesday left for a trip that includes Libya, the target of limited U.N. sanctions, renewing concern at home and abroad he aims to divert Turkey away from the West.

In addition to Tripoli, labelled by Turkey's close ally the United States as a sponsor of terrorism, Erbakan will also visit Egypt and Nigeria, itself something of an international outcast for its hardline approach to political opposition.

A leading figure from the Islamists' coalition partners threatened to resign over the trip to Tripoli. Washington, already leery of modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, has expressed its own disquiet.
"We hope to boost our extremely small commercial relations with Libya and help the participation again for our contractors in tenders there," Erbakan told reporters at the airport.
"This visit is not aimed against any country or society in the world," he said. "America is our friend and ally."

But he noted Turkey was a sovereign state and had to look out for its commercial interests, in this case hundreds of millions of dollars in bad debts due to Turkish contractors and the promise of increased trade.
Increased imports of crude oil from Libya and natural gas from Nigeria are also on the agenda.
"Turkey is an independent country, a democratic country and its leaders have to comply with the wishes of its people," he said.

Interior Minister Mehmet Agar, of the junior partner True Path Party, told Turkish television on Tuesday he was prepared to resign in protest at the Libya visit. The trip has also been targetted by Turkey's mainstream secularist media.
"Naturally. Whatever political traditions require must be done," Agar said when asked whether he would resign over the issue.
He told private channel Show-TV he had refused to sign a decree approving the trip when ministers were asked to sign at a cabinet meeting.
Turkish trade officials have already arrived in Tripoli to seek Libya's payment of outstanding debts of up to $365 million due to Turkish building contractors.
Several dozen Turkish businessmen, including some creditors and others keen for fresh contracts, were to accompany Erbakan.
"Turkish firms have been trying for years to get their debts back," contractor Yasar Ozkan told Reuters. "The prime minister's visit will impress the Libyans more than our years of trying."
Ozkan said the Libyan government owed his firm $3 million. "What right does America have to complain?"

Few foreign leaders have visited Tripoli since the United Nations imposed an air and limited trade embargo on Libya in 1991 for its refusal to hand over two Libyans suspected of blowing up a Pan Am airliner over Lockerbie, Scotland in 1988.
Libya dismissed U.S. criticism of Erbakan's visit. The foreign ministry denounced what it called U.S. "threats and warnings".

On Monday, a U.S. state department spokesman warned NATO-member Turkey to proceed cautiously before improving ties to Libya or Sudan, whose parliamentary speaker the prime minister has reportedly invited to his party congress later in October.
Both countries are on the state department's list of governments that back terrorism.
"We certainly would have concern about any country normalising relations with Sudan and Libya," spokesman Nicholas Burns told a news briefing.
